title: Contrary to Common Belief, The Poorest School Districts Outspend The Wealthiest end-the-wealthiest/
author: Amanda Geduld
summary: A new Brookings study spanning nearly 50 years of Census data finds that high-poverty and predominantly non-white school districts have consistently spent more per student than wealthier districts, challenging the dominant narrative that funding inequality is the root of educational inequality. Researcher Sarah Reber notes these districts face higher labor costs that offset some of the advantage, and argues that how money is spent matters as much as how much is spent. The findings diverge from widely-cited EdBuild data due to methodological differences, particularly the inclusion of federal Title I revenue.
points: Brookings study finds high-poverty districts have outspent wealthier peers per pupil since the early 2000s across all 50 states
Spending across poverty quintiles is U-shaped: poorest and wealthiest districts both spend more than middle-income districts
Higher labor costs in urban areas offset much of the funding advantage for predominantly non-white districts
Findings conflict with EdBuild's 2019 report due to inclusion of federal Title I revenue versus state and local only
Researcher Reber argues the focus should shift from how much schools spend to how productively they spend it
quotes: The findings "raise questions about what I see as a predominant narrative that local property tax finance means that poor schools don't have as much money and that that is a core, structural cause of inequality, and I just think it's not," said Sarah Reber, a senior fellow in economic studies at Brookings and the report's lead author.

They found that spending allocations across these five poverty brackets is U-shaped, with the poorest and wealthiest districts spending the most. Since the early 2000s, the poorest districts have outspent even the wealthiest ones.

The state dictates how much money school districts will receive from the state, and also what the tax policy is for how much you can raise from local taxes," said Sibilia, who is now the executive director of EdFund, a national education research and advocacy nonprofit.

Obviously, there's places that are spending much less and not really getting demonstrably worse outcomes," she said. "I think it's important to try and learn from that and try to figure out what the barriers to being more productive with spending are.

A large body of previous research has looked at differences in spending within states, but in Reber's work she found that the differences across states swamp all of this within-state difference that gets so much attention.
